GHSA-HX59-4HQ9-6VMW.87afc086c9f2f128f59c9b36b004cdc1b32bfe2f:
relay: fix use-after-free and double free on remote buffer (GHSA-hx59-4hq9-6vmw)

A malicious or compromised relay remote could make WeeChat free a buffer
and keep using it: the buffer designated by "buffer_id" was resolved once
before dispatching and reused for every invocation of the event callback.

An array body on "buffer_closed" closed (and freed) the buffer on the
first item, then closed it again on the next items (double free / use
after free); the initial sync could likewise leave the cached pointer
dangling before the "buffer" callback ran.

Search the buffer again immediately before each call to the callback, so
the pointer can never outlive a close. This also covers the initial sync,
since the search happens after obsolete buffers have been closed, and the
callbacks already handle a NULL buffer.

Co-authored-by: mohammed arib <arib@bugqore.com>

GHSA-RFMH-3R7F-JPX5.5078ad909ece8650619859ebc191cbca9681eff3:
irc: fix use-after-free when a batched message disconnects the server (GHSA-rfmh-3r7f-jpx5)

When processing an IRCv3 batch, a batched message can disconnect the
server (for example "ERROR :Closing Link"), which frees all batches
while they are still being processed.

The batch tags are now copied before the messages are dispatched, and
each batch is flagged as processed before being processed, with the list
scanned again from the beginning, to avoid reading or writing freed
memory.

Co-authored-by: mohammed arib <arib@bugqore.com>

GHSA-Q2XG-9GGX-77MR.57c9d49671c9bc75efeb9f6bfa17b14b7ec248cb:
irc: fix stack buffer overflow when splitting a JOIN message (GHSA-q2xg-9ggx-77mr)

irc_message_split_join() built the outgoing JOIN message and the list of
channel keys in two fixed-size stack buffers of 16384 bytes. The strcat calls
appending channels and keys to these buffers were individually guarded against
the buffer size, but the two calls appending the keys to the message
(strcat(msg_to_send, keys_to_add)) were not: when the maximum message length
is greater than 16384 bytes (for example a server advertising a large line
length via message 005), a single split part can hold channels and keys whose
combined length exceeds the buffer, overflowing it on the stack.

Build both strings with dynamic strings (weechat_string_dyn_*) instead of
fixed-size buffers, so there is no size limit and no possible overflow. Add a
regression test splitting a JOIN with a list of channels and keys larger than
16384 bytes.

GHSA-VHV8-G2R9-CWCC.f5fa814fa4bc37ab8dfa9d8f496d14574fc28a81:
core: fix timing attack on TOTP validation (GHSA-vhv8-g2r9-cwcc)

weecrypto_totp_validate compared the generated and client-supplied OTPs
with strcmp and broke out of the time-window loop on the first match.
Both choices leaked information via response timing: strcmp leaked the
expected OTP digit-by-digit (shrinking the brute-force search from
~10^digits to a handful of guesses within the 30-second window), and
the early break leaked which window offset matched.

Compare in constant time with string_memcmp_constant_time and always
iterate the full window, OR-ing the result into otp_ok without an
early exit.

This affects both relay protocols (which call totp_validate via the
public info hook) and any other caller of the info hook.
GHSA-VHV8-G2R9-CWCC.34cbe56a6f04fb8cd085d329dec0f1f9bcd88992:
relay/irc: fix timing attack on PASS command (GHSA-vhv8-g2r9-cwcc)

The IRC relay protocol's PASS handler compared the server password with
the client-supplied value using strcmp, leaking the password byte-by-byte
via response timing. This is the same class of bug fixed for the api and
weechat protocols, on a separate code path that did not go through
relay_auth_check_password_plain.

Extract the HMAC-then-constant-time-compare logic from
relay_auth_check_password_plain into relay_auth_password_equals, then
use it in both the plain-auth wrapper and the IRC PASS handler.
GHSA-VHV8-G2R9-CWCC.a17a80f1d0cf9e73f9d2dd779adf16708b8130a3:
relay: fix timing attack on password authentication (GHSA-vhv8-g2r9-cwcc)

The relay authentication used non-constant-time comparisons (strcasecmp,
strcmp) to verify password hashes and plaintext passwords, allowing an
attacker to derive the expected hash byte-by-byte from response timing
and then authenticate without knowing the password.

- SHA/PBKDF2 hex hash comparisons: normalize the client-supplied hash to
  uppercase and compare in constant time over the fixed expected length.
- Plaintext password comparison: HMAC-SHA256 both passwords with a fresh
  per-call random key and compare the fixed-size MACs in constant time,
  hiding both per-byte timing and the password length.

Add string_memcmp_constant_time helper in core, exposed via the plugin
API. Bump WEECHAT_PLUGIN_API_VERSION accordingly.

GHSA-V2V4-45WM-5CR3.405707d54489b0dfadcaf1392f81d816b2681b7c:
relay: limit size of decompressed websocket frame to prevent memory exhaustion (GHSA-v2v4-45wm-5cr3)

An authenticated relay client using the permessage-deflate websocket
extension could send a small compressed frame that decompresses to an
unbounded amount of data, exhausting all memory and crashing WeeChat.

The output buffer in relay_websocket_inflate is now capped to
WEBSOCKET_INFLATE_MAX_SIZE: frames decompressing beyond this limit are
rejected and the connection is closed.
